query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of carbon dopant into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will increase their glass-forming ability and improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy (e.g., similar to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) synthesized without carbon doping, exhibiting a balance between crystalline and amorphous regions.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a defined, controlled carbon doping step during the alloy synthesis process.
generation.conditions: Under identical rapid cooling and processing conditions, and in systems where phosphorus is already present. Improvement should manifest when the carbon is uniformly distributed and within its solubility limit; effects may be diminished if carbon incorporation is non-uniform or excessive.
generation.structural_mediator: Carbon dopants are expected to disrupt crystalline nucleation by enhancing atomic-scale disorder, thus mediating a more amorphous structure.
generation.mechanism: The added carbon increases structural disorder by interfering with the normal crystalline packing of atoms, thereby impeding nucleation and growth of ordered phases. This results in a higher fraction of the material remaining in the amorphous state and elevates the temperature at which crystallization occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an otherwise similar alloy without carbon doping, the carbon-doped alloy is predicted to have a higher amorphous fraction (i.e., improved glass-forming ability) and a higher crystallization onset temperature, reflecting enhanced thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy synthesized under identical conditions without the carbon doping intervention.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when carbon is incorporated uniformly and at concentrations below the threshold where phase separation or unwanted compounds form. Excessive carbon may negate the benefits or create new phases that deteriorate the desired properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum concentration of carbon and the magnitude of the improvement in glass-forming ability and thermal stability remain to be precisely determined. Variations in processing conditions may also impact the extent of improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples under identical synthesis and rapid-cooling conditions: one with a controlled amount of carbon dopant and one without carbon doping. Characterize both series using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify the amorphous fraction, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the onset of crystallization (thermal stability), and electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to observe the microstructural differences.
measurements: Crystallization onset temperature and exothermic peaks via DSC
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the amorphous fraction and a higher crystallization onset temperature compared to the non-doped baseline, or if they exhibit inferior properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Furthermore, recent findings on NiNbP bulk metallic glasses highlight how phosphorus additions enhance glass-forming ability and increase hardness, albeit at the cost of some ductility []. Inspired by these results, this study explores the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and phase stability of phosphorus-containing alloys to better understand and utilize their unique properties. The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment in these alloys suggests their potential for applications in demanding environments that require enhanced wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties position them as promising candidates for use in the aerospace, automotive, and tooling industries, as well as in advanced coating technologies and high-performance structural components.
